mcqs.question: What does the cut property guarantee, and why does it justify a greedy MST algorithm?
options: It guarantees the MST has exactly V edges for V nodes
It guarantees every edge in the graph belongs to some MST
For any cut splitting the graph into two groups, the minimum-weight edge crossing that cut is guaranteed to be part of some MST — which is exactly the edge a greedy algorithm picks
It guarantees the graph has a unique minimum spanning tree
mcqs.explanation: The cut property specifically says the cheapest edge crossing any cut is safe to include in an MST — and since greedily picking the next-cheapest connecting edge is always picking a minimum crossing edge for the cut between 'already connected' and 'not yet connected,' this is the actual proof that greedy works here. An MST has exactly V-1 edges (not V), not every edge belongs to an MST, and uniqueness only holds when weights are distinct.

mcqs.question: In Kruskal's algorithm, why does checking uf.find(u) != uf.find(v) before adding an edge serve two purposes at once?
options: It only checks for cycles; it has no connection to the cut property or correctness argument
It only ensures the MST has the correct final edge count

It both rejects an edge that would close a cycle (same set) and confirms an accepted edge crosses a valid cut between not-yet-connected pieces (different sets), which is what the cut property requires for correctness
It sorts the edges by weight as a side effect
mcqs.explanation: Same-set means the two endpoints are already connected, so adding the edge would create a cycle; different-set means the edge connects two currently-separate components, which is exactly the crossing-edge condition the cut property needs to guarantee safety. It's doing real double duty here — cycle rejection and correctness justification are the same check, not two separate concerns, and edge count and sorting are unrelated to this specific line.

mcqs.question: Why is an adjacency list, rather than an edge list, the natural fit for Prim's algorithm?
options: Adjacency lists sort automatically by edge weight
Prim's only ever needs to know the edges leaving nodes currently in the growing tree, which is exactly what an adjacency list answers per-node in O(degree)
Edge lists cannot represent weighted edges
Prim's processes the entire graph globally, the same way Kruskal's does
mcqs.explanation: Prim's is node-centric — at every step it only cares about edges leaving the current tree, a query an adjacency list answers directly and efficiently per node. Edge lists represent weights just fine, and Prim's is specifically node-centric (unlike Kruskal's global edge-sort approach), not a global pass over all edges; adjacency lists have no inherent sorting behavior.

mcqs.question: On a dense graph (E close to V^2), which MST algorithm tends to have the edge, and why?
options: Prim's (especially an array-based variant), since Kruskal's O(E log E) sort becomes expensive when E is close to V^2
Kruskal's, since it never needs to consider every edge
Neither algorithm's performance is affected by graph density
Prim's cannot be used on dense graphs at all
mcqs.explanation: When E approaches V^2, Kruskal's edge sort — O(E log E) — becomes expensive purely due to the sheer number of edges, while an array-based Prim's O(V^2) approach (mirroring Dijkstra's dense-graph array variant) avoids that sort cost entirely. Both algorithms' performance is very much density-dependent, and Prim's works perfectly well, often better, on dense graphs.

mcqs.question: A graph has several edges with tied minimum weights. Running Kruskal's and Prim's on this graph produces two different sets of MST edges. Is this a bug?
options: Yes, a correct implementation of either algorithm must always produce the same MST
No — when weights tie, multiple different MSTs with the same total weight can exist, and each algorithm's internal tie-breaking can legitimately pick a different one
Yes, but only Kruskal's implementation could be at fault
No, but only because one of the two algorithms must be implemented incorrectly
mcqs.explanation: MST uniqueness only holds when all edge weights are distinct — with ties, several different edge sets can all achieve the same minimum total weight, and which one each algorithm lands on depends on internal tie-breaking (sort stability, heap ordering), not a defect in either. Expecting identical output across differently-implemented algorithms under tied weights is the actual mistake here.

mcqs.question: A candidate uses Kruskal's algorithm on a graph with 50,000 nodes and roughly 2.4 billion edges (near-complete, very dense). What's the practical concern?
options: Kruskal's will produce an incorrect MST on dense graphs
Kruskal's cannot handle graphs with more than 1 million edges at all
Union-Find becomes incorrect once the edge count exceeds the node count significantly
Sorting roughly 2.4 billion edges is a heavy, avoidable cost — an array-based Prim's O(V^2) approach would sidestep that sort entirely and likely run faster here
mcqs.explanation: Kruskal's is still correct on a dense graph, but sorting billions of edges is a real, avoidable cost — an array-based Prim's, which never needs a global sort and instead scans O(V) per step, would likely be markedly faster on a graph this dense. There's no hard edge-count ceiling on Kruskal's, and Union-Find's correctness has nothing to do with the ratio of edges to nodes.
